He May Be The First Documented Trebuchet Victim The victim's injuries resemble those from a high-speed car crash, only this was the Middle Ages. Something hit the young man from behind with such extraordinary force that his skull broke in 61 places. His ribs cracked in jagged zigzags. His shoulder, spine and limbs fractured. Whatever struck him appears to have knocked him from his feet almost instantly. More than 700 years later, researchers think they know what could have done it: a large stone hurled by a trebuchet. The man, known simply as Skeleton 150, was unearthed beneath the chapel at Scotland’s Stirling Castle in 1997. A new analysis identified 167 fractures, most sustained at or around the time of death. Researchers argue that the unusual distribution of damage points to a single, exceptionally crushing impact — perhaps making this the first known archaeological evidence of a person killed by a trebuchet. Stirling Castle was famously besieged in 1304 by King Edward I of England, whose forces built an enormous trebuchet known as the War Wolf. The timing fits. The injuries fit. Yet whether Skeleton 150 actually met the legendary weapon is much harder to prove definitively. A Death Written Across the Skeleton Jo Buckberry, a biological anthropologist at the University of Bradford, and Patrick Randolph-Quinney of Uppsala University examined Skeleton 150 using X-rays, microscopy and micro-CT scanning. Their findings were presented this month at the 25th European Meeting of the Paleopathology Association in Berlin. The man was between 22 and 34 years old at the time of death. Researchers counted 61 fractures in his skull and 57 in his ribs, along with extensive damage to his vertebrae, arms and right shoulder. Most of the destruction clustered around the back of his head and his right shoulder. “This is not what I’m used to seeing,” Buckberry said during her presentation. Initially, the damage did not necessarily look like evidence of violence. When archaeologists excavated the remains, some suspected that the bones had simply broken after burial. But newer imaging techniques allowed Buckberry and her colleagues to distinguish brittle damage to old bone from fractures suffered while bone was still fresh. Get smarter every day... Stay ahead with ZME Science and subscribe. Thank you! One more thing... Please check your inbox and confirm your subscription. The pieces fit together like a gruesome three-dimensional puzzle. The force appears to have struck from behind, concentrating around his right shoulder and the back of his head before driving him violently to the ground. The researchers concluded that a single high-speed impact best explained the injuries. Buckberry found the closest modern comparison in forensic cases involving cars and trains. A horse, cart or fall from the castle walls did not produce a convincing match. In medieval Scotland, that leaves one rather conspicuous suspect. The King Who Brought 13 Siege Engines A counterweight trebuchet exploited the force of gravity to produce artillery. A huge weight dropped at one end of a long wooden arm, whipping the other end upward and releasing a stone from a sling. Large versions could throw rocks weighing tens or even hundreds of kilograms far enough to batter fortifications. And in 1304, Stirling Castle was receiving plenty of them. The castle represented one of the last centers of Scottish resistance to Edward I during the First War of Scottish Independence. Its position on a rocky outcrop made it extraordinarily difficult to attack. According to Historic Environment Scotland’s account of the siege , Edward assembled 13 catapults and trebuchets, which bombarded the fortress day and night for roughly three months. The scale of the operation was remarkable. Scottish churches were ordered to surrender lead from their roofs. Thirty-nine cartloads arrived from Brechin, Dunfermline and St Andrews, while Glasgow supplied iron and large stones. About 25 defenders, commanded by Sir William Oliphant, remained inside. Then Edward escalated. The War Wolf Five master carpenters and 50 workmen assembled an immense new trebuchet, the War Wolf. It is believed to be the largest trebuchet in history. Oliphant reportedly tried to surrender before the machine could be used. Edward refused. When a roughly 140-kilogram projectile was finally launched, Historic Environment Scotland says it shattered part of the castle’s curtain wall. That makes the War Wolf an enticing candidate for Skeleton 150’s death — but perhaps too enticing. “It’s difficult to say whether or not the War Wolf was the weapon that caused the death of the individual,” Buckberry told Live Science . The other siege engines had been bombarding the castle for months. Since the War Wolf arrived late, one of the earlier machines is statistically more likely to be the culprit. Medieval Warfare Left Different Signatures in Bone Archaeologists have reconstructed violent medieval deaths before. Cuts from swords and axes, punctures from pointed weapons and arrow injuries can all leave recognizable traces. A large 2021 study of skeletal trauma in medieval Cambridge , for instance, showed how fractures can preserve evidence of accidents, dangerous work and interpersonal violence centuries after death. Skeleton 150 is different because his injuries do not resemble a conventional weapon wound. Instead, much of his upper body appears to have failed at once. “While the use of siege engines is well documented, we believe this is the first evidence of trebuchet trauma in the archaeological record,” Buckberry and Randolph-Quinney wrote in their conference abstract . There is an important caveat. No stone was found embedded in the man, and the researchers acknowledge that there are almost no directly comparable forensic cases. The diagnosis therefore rests on the fracture pattern, the enormous force required to create it and the historical context rather than on a projectile that researchers could tie to a particular machine. Still, an outside expert found the case persuasive. “It’s convincing,” Lukas Waltenberger, a forensic osteologist at Vilnius University who was not involved in the work, told Science . “It seems like a high-velocity, high-force, high-speed impact in a short amount of time.” For centuries, chronicles described trebuchets in terms of the walls they demolished. Skeleton 150 may provide a gruesome record of what happened when a human being stood in the path of one. Tibi Puiu Tibi is a science journalist and co-founder of ZME Science. He writes mainly about emerging tech, physics, climate, and space. In his spare time, Tibi likes to make weird music on his computer and groom felines. He has a B.Sc in mechanical engineering and an M.Sc in renewable energy systems. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy0z.text: Image source, STR/EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, The artwork was first spotted in an estate agent's photo advertising a property near Buenos Aires, Argentina By James Gregory Published 2 hours ago A painting which was stolen by the Nazis and only recovered in Argentina last year must now be returned to the heir of its rightful owner, a court has ruled. The late-baroque Portrait of a Lady was lost for 80 years until it was spotted in photographs of a house for sale near Buenos Aires. The house belonged to Patricia Kadgien, the daughter of a Nazi fugitive who had fled there after the Second World War, and she has now agreed to return the painting in exchange for not being prosecuted for concealing it from the authorities. Portrait of a Lady was among over 1,000 artworks looted from the collection of Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker after the Nazi invasion of the Netherlands in 1940. His daughter-in-law and sole heir Marei von Saher intends for the painting to be exhibited on a temporary loan at the Holocaust Museum of Buenos Aires to spread awareness of the issue, Argentine newspaper Clarin reports. Von Saher has previously said her family "aims to bring back every single artwork robbed from Jacques' collection, and to restore his legacy". This painting was first recognised in August 2025 by the Dutch Algemeen Dagblad (AD) newspaper on an estate agent's website of a property in the coastal town of Mar del Plata. It was hanging above a green sofa in the living room of Patricia Kadgien, whose father Friedrich Kadgien had been a top adviser to Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler's deputy. Goring plundered thousands of works across Europe. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Patricia Kadgien and her husband Juan Carlos Cortegoso appeared alongside their lawyer in a court near Buenos Aires on Friday Last September, Patricia Kadgien and her husband were charged with concealment and placed under house arrest after a search of her property initially failed to find the painting. But at Friday's hearing in Mar del Plata, all criminal proceedings were suspended against the couple. The agreement reached between the families and prosecutors means Kadgien and her husband will give up all rights to the artwork and must donate 4.8 million pesos (Â£2,356; $3,185) to local hospitals. Portrait of a Lady, also known as Contessa Colleoni, is attributed to the work of the late-baroque artist Giuseppe Ghislandi. However, experts have questioned the artwork's provenance, with some scholars attributing it to Giacomo Ceruti - another Italian artist from the same period. https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/.text: Tens of thousands of Hasidim from around the world are flocking to Ukraine ahead of Rosh Hashanah to visit the grave of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov in the city of Uman. According to data from the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine (SBGS), more than 31,000 Hasidim have entered the country in organized groups since the end of August, with the heaviest traffic recorded in recent days. Ukrainian Border Guard spokesman Andriy Demchenko said that the greatest congestion at border crossings was recorded over the past two to three days. “On Wednesday alone, approximately 13,700 Hasidim entered the country, while another 11,600 entered during the two preceding days," Demchenko said. The spokesman also noted that the pilgrims’ travel routes have shifted in recent days, with most traffic now concentrated at Ukraine’s land border crossings with Poland and Romania, alongside the crossings with Moldova. Footage circulated on social media in recent days showed long lines at border crossings between Poland and Ukraine. The Ukrainian Border Guard clarified that these are temporary periods of congestion caused by the arrival of buses carrying organized groups, and that the lines are processed and cleared quickly. According to Ukrainian authorities, the pilgrims are entering the country as planned and without unusual incidents, with the exception of a small number of cases in which 13 foreign nationals who did not meet the legal requirements were denied entry. Ukrainian authorities estimate that approximately 40,000 people will arrive in Uman for the holiday this year.
